title: Lecture 01
text:
Why R and not Python?

The basic difference: R was built by statisticians for statisticians, so the focus is narrower.
Python was built by software engineers for general purpose applications, so the focus is broad.
R is great for focusing on thinking about statistical problems, solving them, and communicating the results
Python is great for doing lots of different things. Example, download thousands of YouTube videos, analyze the images frame by frame, transcribe the sound into words, analyze the data, etc.

title: Lecture 01
text:
Why R and not Python? (cont’d)

R is “Problem-First” or “Problem-Forward”
In R, data structures are integrated directly into the language and do not require additional tools (but tools, found in libraries, are helpful).
When you load a dataset, R assumes you want to analyze it. The syntax is designed to mirror the way a researcher thinks: “I want to study something which involves data, get the data, then filter/subset it, then group it, then summarize/describe, then model, etc.”

Also R’s simpler modeling formulas allows one to remain thinking about the analytical problem.

title: Lecture 01
text:
Why R and not Python? (cont’d)

Python is “System-First”
In Python, you “build” your environment before you can solve the problem (importing tools, found in libraries such as pandas, numpy, etc.)
In Python, it matters how your programming code integrates within a larger system, the result is versatility. So it is easy for Python to interact with YouTube for example (not as easy/or maybe not possible in R)
In R, what matters is how the programming code helps you reveal the truth found in the data.

title: Lecture 01
text:
The “Formula” vs. “The Matrix”
In R, a statistical model is treated like a scientific hypothesis. In Python, a statistical model is treated like “how does the computer wants its input formatted?”

R Approach: You use formulas (y ~ x). This is like saying “I think \(y\) changes in response to \(x\).” R automatically handles things creating the underlying matrix and keeps the names of your variables intact so you can read the results.
Python Approach: Most Python libraries(toolkits) require you to manually transform your data into a matrix of numbers first. Then pass them in as \(x\) and \(y\).

In R, the code looks like the math inside your head. In Python, the code looks like the way the computer understands math.

title: Lecture 01
text:
R v Python Example 2
R allows for a more linear flow of thought, less engineering, more thinking. Not good or bad, just a different philosophy. In each of these examples, we filter (subset/split up), aggregate (combine), then analyze:

RPythonPython with pandasPython one line


R uses the “pipe” operator (%>% Tidyverse library or |> core R) which is read like “then”. You know zero R today, but with a little help, you can read your R code like a sentence.
library(dplyr)                    # a library is like a toolbox filled with helpful functions
df %>%                            # df stands for "data frame", you'll learn more about this data structure soon 
  filter(year > 2020) %>%         # filter() function - keep these years in the data frame
  group_by(state) %>%             # Then, "group the data by" state for analysis
  summarize(mean_yield = mean(y)) # Finally, calculate the mean() save it to a new variable mean_yield
We created a new variable just by naming it.


In Python, you frequently create “intermediate” variables or use complex nested brackets to do the same:
from collections import defaultdict

## filter
filtered = [row for row in data if row["year"] > 2020]

## group and accumulate sums and counts
sums = defaultdict(float)
counts = defaultdict(int)

for row in filtered:
    state = row["state"]
    y = row["y"]
    sums[state] += y
    counts[state] += 1

## compute means
mean_yield_by_state = {
    state: sums[state] / counts[state]
    for state in sums
}

## print the result
for state, mean_yield in mean_yield_by_state.items():
    print(state, mean_yield)


This is why pandas exists (compare Python using pandas against the previous Python no pandas)
import pandas as pd

## assume df is a data frame in Python
result = (
    df[df["year"] > 2020]          ## Keep these years
      .groupby("state", as_index=False) ## aggregate by state  
      .agg(mean_yield=("y", "mean"))  ## Calculate the mean of y and store as mean_yield
)

print(result)

title: A note on R objects and their names
text:
from Chapter 2.2 “Binding Basics”
Consider this code:

x <- c(1, 2, 3)

It’s easy to read it as: “create an object named ‘x’, containing the values 1, 2, and 3”. ( or R object ‘x’ gets the vector 1, 2, 3 ) Unfortunately, that’s a simplification that will lead to inaccurate predictions about what R is actually doing behind the scenes. It’s more accurate to say that this code is doing two things:

It’s creating an object, a vector of values, c(1, 2, 3).
And it’s binding (associating) that object to a name, x.

In other words, the object, or value, (technically) doesn’t have a name; it’s actually the name x here that has a value 1, 2, 3.
To further clarify this distinction, I’ll draw diagrams like this:








The name, x, is drawn with a rounded rectangle. It has an arrow that points to (or binds or references) the value, the vector c(1, 2, 3). The arrow points in opposite direction to the assignment arrow: <- creates a binding from the name on the left-hand side to the object on the right-hand side.
Thus, you can think of a name as a reference to a value. For example, if you run this code, you don’t get another copy of the value c(1, 2, 3), you get another binding to the existing object:

y <- x









You might have noticed that the value c(1, 2, 3) has a label: 0x74b. While the vector doesn’t have a name, I’ll occasionally need to refer to an object independent of its bindings. To make that possible, I’ll label values with a unique identifier. These identifiers have a special form that looks like the object’s memory “address”, i.e. the location in memory where the object is stored. But because the actual memory addresses changes every time the code is run, we use these identifiers instead.
You can access an object’s identifier with lobstr::obj_addr(). Doing so allows you to see that both x and y point to the same identifier:

obj_addr(x)

[1] "0x14258d6c8"

obj_addr(y)

[1] "0x14258d6c8"


These identifiers are long, and change every time you restart R.
It can take some time to get your head around the distinction between names and values, but understanding this is really helpful in functional programming where functions can have different names in different contexts.
(end Wickham)

title: A note on R objects and their names
text:
The result of R’s ways
So take a look at what happens when we modify one but not the other

y[[3]] <- 4   ## I am following Wickham's style here, 

## instead you could have used y[3] <- 4 
## read as "y's third element" gets 4
## because we have simple vector, in other places 
## y[[3]] <- 4 is clearer, but we're not there yet

x

[1] 1 2 3

y

[1] 1 2 4


let’s check the memory locations

obj_addr(x)

[1] "0x14258d6c8"

obj_addr(y)

[1] "0x114e06f78"


(start Wickham again)
Modifying y clearly didn’t modify x. So what happened to the shared binding? While the value associated with y changed, the original object did not. Instead, R created a new object, 0xcd2, a copy of 0x74b with one value changed, then rebound y to that object.








This behaviour is called copy-on-modify. Understanding it will radically improve your intuition about the performance of R code.
(end Wickham)
Do you need to completely understand this to do well in Stats 20? Probably not BUT if you decide to learn Python or become a paid R programmer later (because all of the documentation assumes you understand R’s decision making in memory), it would help to understand what he is trying to tell you in Chapter 2 of the textbook Advanced R.

title: Lecture 06
text:
List
From the original documentation

Lists are another kind of data storage. Lists have elements, each of which can contain any type of R object, i.e. the elements of a list do not have to be of the same type. List elements are accessed through three different indexing operations. These are explained in detail in Indexing.

Lists are called “generic vectors”, and the basic vector types (e.g., integer, numeric, character etc.) that we have been using are referred to as “atomic vectors”.

title: Lecture 06
text:
Recall

The data type in our simple vector must be all the same (all numeric, all character, all logical)
If there is mixing, we say that R “coerces” the vector to be one type.
But if data are stored in a list, they can maintain their own type.

section: Why do they do this? Why lists?
text:
Why do they do this? Why lists?

If a programmer wants a single long and complex structure and also wants each piece of it to keep its original type, they use a list to contain all of the pieces.
Recall vectors (atomic ones) coerce the data to keep the type with the highest priority (e.g., logical coerces to integer, integer to numeric, numeric to character etc.)
Many important model objects are lists, like the results of a regression and more advanced models.
Many heavily used functions produce lists

text:
Solution (Week 3)

Remove non-numeric characters first, then convert to numeric.
We could remove the characters (like the comma and percentage) in this manner
gsub is a “global substitution” function, it searches for the character we specify and then removes all occurrences.
might be easiest understood reading from the innermost part of the R function


# for commas |> is a "pipe
# The pipe |> means:
# “Take the result on the left and pass it into the function on the right.”"

BOM0024$Worldwide <- gsub(",", "", BOM0024$Worldwide) |> as.numeric()
BOM0024$Domestic  <- gsub(",", "", BOM0024$Domestic) |> as.numeric()
BOM0024$Foreign   <- gsub(",", "", BOM0024$Foreign) |> as.numeric()

# for percent we nested it instead to show the readability of |>
BOM0024$Domestic_percent <- (gsub("%", "", BOM0024$Domestic_percent) |> as.numeric())/100

Functions do all of the work in R. Functions have a function name followed by parentheses. Functions can have arguments and options within the parentheses. In this case, we have measurements of different parts of the iris flower (sepal length, sepal width, petal length, petal width) and the species of the flower.

The vector
In the example of x, y and z, a numeric vector is a sequence of values that are all of the same type (in this case, numbers). In R, the vector (there are different types, later…) is the fundamental data structure.
Notice that for a single number, R still treats it as a vector of length 1 (there are no scalars in R) with index [1]. This is a common source of confusion for those new to R. R is 1-indexed, meaning enumeration starts at 1. It is like the way we count. Python, C / C++, Java, JavaScript and many other programming languages are 0-indexed, meaning enumeration starts at 0.
You can examine the built-in data set rivers to see an example of a numeric vector. Try it out below and notice the values of the indices between the [].

title: Week 1 Getting Started
text:
Takeaways

R is a fancy calculator that can do basic arithmetic and more complex calculations. Issue a help("Syntax") to see the syntax for basic calculations in R.
R uses line breaks to separate the outputs of different calculations (or complete each expression generally).

You can give a value a name (called a variable, like math), and then use that name (variable) in calculations and to store results.
R has many built-in data sets such as iris and rivers that you can use to practice your data manipulation and analysis skills.
Functions do all of the work in R. They have arguments that you can modify to get different results. For example, head() is a function that takes an R (typically) data object as an argument (it can take other kinds of R objects).
The is() function tells you what type of R object you are working with.
The vector is the most basic type of data object in R, and it is a sequence of values that are all of the same type.
The data frame is a more complex type of R object that consists of multiple vectors (columns) that can be of different types (numbers, factors, etc.).
R vectors are 1-indexed (numbered starting with 1), even when the vector only has one value (there are no scalars in R, only vectors).
The str() function gives you a quick overview of the structure of an R object.
The summary() function gives you a quick summary of the data in each vector (column) of a data frame.

Simplistic but useful “rule”: everything in R is an object.

An object is storage space (memory) with an associated name.

title: Lecture 03
text:
Names are (R?) Important

R is case sensitive so the name junk is different from JUNK or juNk.
R object names should start with a period OR a letter (and nothing else)
so .first_value is a valid R object name and if a name starts with a period, a letter should follow.
Variables and functions that you create have names with only lowercase letters, numbers, and _. Use underscores (_) (so called snake case) to separate words within a name. For example: this_is_my_first_variable <- 1:1000
While periods are legal, you may wish to avoid using them because R uses them to name its own functions and variables.
R object names can have spaces and start with periods and numbers, but these names need to be quoted with backticks to be used. So if you have a variable name like Zip Code, when you access it, you will need to call it using `Zip Code`.
The overall goal is to be understood when sharing code. So clarity, readability and following common conventions are useful. The habit of good naming hygiene is important for Stats 102ABC.

Element-wise execution in R can be treacherous because base R will perform math even when vectors differ in length (some packages prevent this from happening).

If the lengths of your vectors differ, the result of the expression is a vector with the same length as the longest vector which occurs in the expression.

title: Lecture 03
text:
Coercion

Types againLogicalInt/NumLogical/CharNum/Char



Recall there are different data types, when combining types, R follows a hierarchy


Logical (TRUE/FALSE) is the lowest
Integer
Numeric (double)
Complex (probably not in Stats 20)
Character
Factor (later)
Raw (not in Stats 20) is the highest

When you combine different types of vectors, R will coerce them to the type that is higher in the hierarchy. Some functions in R behave this way – coercing data types to suit its needs.



Logical (TRUE/FALSE) occupies the bottom of the hierarchy, it’s always coerced if combined with any non-Logical type of data.


logical_vector <- c(TRUE, FALSE)
integer_vector <- 1:10 # colon operator generates integers

title: Lecture 05
text:
For your consideration

In assembly, we must tell the computer every tiny step. Assembly required humans to think/communicate like machines.
In R, Python, and other modern languages, we write what we want in a compact and more natural form
Programming languages evolved to let humans think less about machine details and more about ideas, data, and problems.
LLMs are part of the same long arc of evolution. They allow us to express intent in ordinary language. So “please add 2 and 5” as in the previous slide
Assembly -> C -> Python -> LLMs(?) older languages were not completely replaced – but their application may be narrower

title: Lecture 07
section: The Logic of Constructing Plots in R
text:
The Logic of Constructing Plots in R

The functions on the previous slide could be roughly categorized in “high level” and “low level” functions.
A plot is created in base R graphics by first calling a high-level function.
A high-level graphics function can create a plot and does not require any other function to precede it
A low-level graphics function are called to add more output to the plot (such as additional lines or points). These functions depend on a previous high-level function.
Plots created in base R are layered like a cake. We initialize a plot with a high level function and then layer it with additional information provided by low level functions

two specific vectors from many

You must specify them, x first, then y (unless you use argument names x= and y=). Extraction is an important skill. All 3 lines below will give exactly the same plot:


op <- par()
par(mfrow = c(2, 2))

plot(iris$Sepal.Length, iris$Sepal.Width, main = "No argument names") 
# works but bad for communication

plot(x = iris$Sepal.Length, y = iris$Sepal.Width, main = "Argument names") 
# 102 happy place, named and in order

plot(y = iris$Sepal.Width, x = iris$Sepal.Length, main = "Argument names, any order") 
# always clear when you use argument naming

par(op)

The ... suggests even more potential options not fully documented. So if you include an argument that plot() does recognize, it passes it along to associated other functions. Problem is, R doesn’t necessarily tell you if it’s completely unrecognized, things just don’t happen.

title: Lecture 07
text:
plot() help - arguments
Arguments:

    x, y: the ‘x’ and ‘y’ arguments provide the x and y coordinates for
          the plot.  Any reasonable way of defining the coordinates is
          acceptable.  See the function ‘xy.coords’ for details.  If
          supplied separately, they must be of the same length.

    type: 1-character string giving the type of plot desired.  The
          following values are possible, for details, see ‘plot’: ‘"p"’
          for points, ‘"l"’ for lines, ‘"b"’ for both points and lines,
          ‘"c"’ for empty points joined by lines, ‘"o"’ for overplotted
          points and lines, ‘"s"’ and ‘"S"’ for stair steps and ‘"h"’
          for histogram-like vertical lines.  Finally, ‘"n"’ does not
          produce any points or lines.

    xlim: the x limits (x1, x2) of the plot.  Note that ‘x1 > x2’ is
          allowed and leads to a ‘reversed axis’.

          The default value, ‘NULL’, indicates that the range of the
          finite values to be plotted should be used.

    ylim: the y limits of the plot.

     log: a character string which contains ‘"x"’ if the x axis is to
          be logarithmic, ‘"y"’ if the y axis is to be logarithmic and
          ‘"xy"’ or ‘"yx"’ if both axes are to be logarithmic.

    main: a main title for the plot, see also ‘title’.

     sub: a subtitle for the plot.

    xlab: a label for the x axis, defaults to a description of ‘x’.

    ylab: a label for the y axis, defaults to a description of ‘y’.

     ann: a logical value indicating whether the default annotation
          (title and x and y axis labels) should appear on the plot.

    axes: a logical value indicating whether both axes should be drawn
          on the plot.  Use graphical parameter ‘"xaxt"’ or ‘"yaxt"’ to
          suppress just one of the axes.

frame.plot: a logical indicating whether a box should be drawn around
          the plot.

panel.first: an ‘expression’ to be evaluated after the plot axes are
          set up but before any plotting takes place.  This can be
          useful for drawing background grids or scatterplot smooths.
          Note that this works by lazy evaluation: passing this
          argument from other ‘plot’ methods may well not work since it
          may be evaluated too early.

panel.last: an expression to be evaluated after plotting has taken
          place but before the axes, title and box are added.  See the
          comments about ‘panel.first’.

     asp: the y/x aspect ratio, see ‘plot.window’.
     xgap.axis, ygap.axis: the x/y axis gap factors, passed as ‘gap.axis’ to
          the two ‘axis()’ calls (when ‘axes’ is true, as per default).

     ...: other graphical parameters (see ‘par’ and section ‘Details’
          below).

title: Lecture 07
text:
plot() help - details
Details:

     Commonly used graphical parameters are:

     ‘col’ The colors for lines and points.  Multiple colors can be
          specified so that each point can be given its own color.  If
          there are fewer colors than points they are recycled in the
          standard fashion.  Lines will all be plotted in the first
          colour specified.

     ‘bg’ a vector of background colors for open plot symbols, see
          ‘points’.  Note: this is *not* the same setting as
          ‘par("bg")’.

     ‘pch’ a vector of plotting characters or symbols: see ‘points’.

     ‘cex’ a numerical vector giving the amount by which plotting
          characters and symbols should be scaled relative to the
          default.  This works as a multiple of ‘par("cex")’.  ‘NULL’
          and ‘NA’ are equivalent to ‘1.0’.  Note that this does not
          affect annotation: see below.

     ‘lty’ a vector of line types, see ‘par’.

     ‘cex.main’, ‘col.lab’, ‘font.sub’, etc settings for main- and

Colors

R has 657 built-in colors, (see colors() )many more can be created using other libraries. These are colors R recognizes by name.
There are 3 basic settings used in base R graphics: col=, fg= and bg=

col= is used for the colors of lines, symbols and text
fg= specifies the colors of axes and borders
bg= specifies the color of the background or fill

There are several specific settings such as col.main= for the plot title, col.axis = for the axis labels etc.
You can specify colors by name, by hexadecimal code, and by number.
You can find color specifications everywhere and generate a version that R can use example: UCLA Colors
You can find websites to help you choose specific colors

title: Lecture 07
text:
Adding and modifying lines

lty= controls the linetype, from the documentation:
1-character string giving the type of plot desired. The following values are possible, for details, see plot:

“p” for points,
“l” for lines,
“b” for both points and lines,
“c” for empty points joined by lines,
“o” for overplotted points and lines,
“s” and “S” for stair steps and
“h” for histogram-like vertical lines.


Finally, “n” does not produce any points or lines.

lwd= controls the line width, so lwd= 2 means twice the default thickness
See ?plot.default for a deeper dive

title: Lecture 07
text:
Example

This is a financial data package and we will use it to generate multiple lines to plot.


#install.packages("quantmod")
suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(quantmod))

# Fetch data for the last 90 days 
getFX("EUR/USD", from = Sys.Date() - 90) # Sys.Date() is today's date
getFX("GBP/USD", from = Sys.Date() - 90)
getFX("CHF/USD", from = Sys.Date() - 90)
getFX("CAD/USD", from = Sys.Date() - 90)

# Merge them into one dataset for plotting
currency_data <- merge(EURUSD, GBPUSD, CHFUSD, CADUSD)
# head(currency_data) # always check

# multiple lines
plot(x = index(currency_data),  # index values, dates here
     y = currency_data[,1],   # first currency
     ylim = range(currency_data), # makes sure the y-axis is large enough to accommodate the possible values
     type = "l",  # line type - solid
     lwd= 1.5,   # line thickness, 1.5 times default
     main="Currency Trends (Last 2 Months) vs USD", 
     col="blue", 
     ylab="Exchange Rate")
# we add "low-level" graphical functions, lines()
lines(index(currency_data), currency_data[,2], col="red", lwd= 1.5)
lines(index(currency_data), currency_data[,3], col="green", lwd= 1.5)
lines(index(currency_data), currency_data[,4], col="magenta", lwd= 1.5)
legend("right", legend=c("EUR", "GBP", "CHF", "CAD"), 
       col=c("blue", "red", "green", "magenta"), lty= 1, lwd= 1.5, cex= 0.6)

title: Lecture 07
text:
filtering in base R

An important skill and when we examine the Tidyverse, you can judge
Let’s suppose we think ‘we will drop the least popular’
In base R filtering means:


Keep rows where a condition is TRUE.

Everything comes back to this fundamental pattern:
df[ some_condition , ]

read “we have a dataframe (df) extract some_condition is TRUE all the columns”

title: Lecture 07
text:
Application

Suppose we want to keep those tracks which have a popularity of at least 1 because we noticed about 10% of songs had a popularity of zero.
Our condition translated into R, looks like

spotify_songs$track_popularity >= 1
or
spotify_songs$track_popularity > 0

Unfortunately, if you only ran this, R would return a vector with as many rows as spotify_songs but full of TRUE and FALSE (try it, you’ll see)
BUT when we insert it into a dataframe extract:

spotify_songs[spotify_songs$track_popularity >= 1, ]

R will respond by keeping only those rows for which this condition is true and give us the filtered data frame that we want to use.

title: Lecture 07
text:
Make it real

# our conditioning variable
fivenum(spotify_songs$track_popularity)

[1]   0  24  45  62 100

# filter with a condition
spotify_filtered <- spotify_songs[spotify_songs$track_popularity >= 1, ]

# always check
fivenum(spotify_filtered$track_popularity)

[1]   1  31  48  63 100



Now plot it


plot(x = spotify_filtered$duration_ms, y = spotify_filtered$track_popularity,
     main = "Filtered and possibly more useless than ever")

The table() function is ancient but easy and useful. Especially when trying to build data for plots
from the documentation, simplified

table(...,
      exclude = if (useNA == "no") c(NA, NaN),
      useNA = c("no", "ifany", "always"),
      dnn = list.names(...), deparse.level = 1)

...        one or more objects which can be interpreted as factors (including numbers or character strings), or a list (such as a data frame) whose components can be so interpreted.

title: Lecture 07
text:
Takeaway for the Heatmap

A heat map is a just tool like the others tools
It is a scaled matrix of numerical values represented by colors
They represent Z-scores (standard deviations from the mean of the column)

text:
R v Python Example 2
R allows for a more linear flow of thought, less engineering, more thinking. Not good or bad, just a different philosophy. In each of these examples, we filter (subset/split up), aggregate (combine), then analyze:

RPythonPython with pandasPython one line


R uses the “pipe” operator (%>% Tidyverse library or |> core R) which is read like “then”. You know zero R today, but with a little help, you can read your R code like a sentence.
library(dplyr)                    # a library is like a toolbox filled with helpful functions
df %>%                            # df stands for "data frame", you'll learn more about this data structure soon 
  filter(year > 2020) %>%         # filter() function - keep these years in the data frame
  group_by(state) %>%             # Then, "group the data by" state for analysis
  summarize(mean_yield = mean(y)) # Finally, calculate the mean() save it to a new variable mean_yield
We created a new variable just by naming it.


In Python, you frequently create “intermediate” variables or use complex nested brackets to do the same:
from collections import defaultdict

## filter
filtered = [row for row in data if row["year"] > 2020]

## group and accumulate sums and counts
sums = defaultdict(float)
counts = defaultdict(int)

for row in filtered:
    state = row["state"]
    y = row["y"]
    sums[state] += y
    counts[state] += 1

## compute means
mean_yield_by_state = {
    state: sums[state] / counts[state]
    for state in sums
}

## print the result
for state, mean_yield in mean_yield_by_state.items():
    print(state, mean_yield)


This is why pandas exists (compare Python using pandas against the previous Python no pandas)
import pandas as pd

## assume df is a data frame in Python
result = (
    df[df["year"] > 2020]          ## Keep these years
      .groupby("state", as_index=False) ## aggregate by state  
      .agg(mean_yield=("y", "mean"))  ## Calculate the mean of y and store as mean_yield
)

print(result)

The American Statistical Association emphasizes computational thinking because modern statistics is no longer just formulas on paper:

Simulation > closed-form solutions (formulas)

Reproducible pipelines > one time calculations/analyses
Data wrangling > textbook-clean datasets

statistical thinking + computational thinking = data science.

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

plt.close("all")

import statsmodels.api as sm

mtcars = sm.datasets.get_rdataset("mtcars").data
X = sm.add_constant(mtcars["wt"])
y = mtcars["mpg"]
model = sm.OLS(y, X).fit()

# 2. Setup Figure
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 5))

# Plot the points (open circles like R)
ax.scatter(model.fittedvalues, model.resid, facecolors='none', edgecolors='black')

# Add the horizontal 'zero' line
ax.axhline(0, color='silver', linestyle=':', zorder=0)

# 3. Add the Red Lowess Line (The 'R' special)
lowess = sm.nonparametric.lowess(model.resid, model.fittedvalues, frac=2/3)
ax.plot(lowess[:, 0], lowess[:, 1], color='red', lw=1, alpha=0.8)

# 4. Label the Top 3 Outliers
# Find indices of the 3 largest absolute residuals
top_3_idx = np.abs(model.resid).sort_values(ascending=False).head(3).index

for i in top_3_idx:
    ax.annotate(i, (model.fittedvalues[i], model.resid[i]), 
                xytext=(5, 5), textcoords='offset points', fontsize=9)

# Formatting
ax.set_title("Residuals vs Fitted")
ax.set_xlabel("Fitted values")
ax.set_ylabel("Residuals")
plt.savefig("01_residuals_vs_fitted.png")
